hypothesis: The unannotated lipid-fraction feature with molecular formula C30H30N4O3 is increased/characteristic in stool of 5-month-old infants relative to 12-month-old infants.
rationale: This feature is identified only by a molecular formula (C30H30N4O3) from an untargeted lipidomics platform, with no compound name, database identifier (HMDB/LIPID MAPS/KEGG), or structural class assignment. Searches on the formula itself returned only chemical-catalog and patent-compound entries (e.g., a PubChem entry for a patent example compound, an Oakwood catalog bis-hydrazone, KNApSAcK plant-metabolite records) with no biological, fecal, gut-microbiome, or infant context whatsoever. No primary study - human or animal - was found reporting this formula, or any named compound plausibly assigned to it, as differing between younger (~5 month, pre-/early complementary feeding) and older (~12 month, established complementary feeding) infants. The only relevant literature located is generic and feature-agnostic: untargeted infant fecal metabolomics/lipidomics studies show that many lipid-fraction features shift substantially across the complementary feeding transition between ~5-6 and 12 months, with milk-derived/breastmilk- or formula-associated features generally higher earlier and diet-diversification-associated features higher later (PLOS One complementary feeding cohort; npj Metab Health Dis 1- and 6-month feeding-pattern metabolome study; a bioRxiv network-learning analysis of 5-12 month formula-fed infant fecal metabolomics). Note also that the formula has 18 double-bond equivalents and 4 nitrogens, which is atypical for a conventional acyl lipid and is more consistent with a highly conjugated/polycyclic nitrogenous compound (e.g., a tetrapyrrole-like or exogenous/xenobiotic species); however, it does not match bilirubin (C33H36N4O6), biliverdin, or urobilinoids, so even the plausible-analogy argument (fecal bilirubinoids being high in young infants before bilirubin-reductase-carrying microbes colonize, as described in the BilR Nature Microbiology work) is speculative and cannot be attached to this feature. This is therefore theoretical/pathway-level plausibility only - no feature-specific evidence in either direction, and no contradicting evidence - which maps to a score of 1 rather than 0 (something relevant to the age contrast was found) and clearly not 2 or 3 (no study addresses this feature).

evidence.title: Adaptation of the infant gut microbiome during the complementary feeding transition
evidence.study_population: Human infants followed longitudinally across the complementary feeding transition (approximately 5-12 months of age), fecal microbiome and metabolome
evidence.relevance: Generic, non-feature-specific support that fecal lipid-class metabolite features change systematically with age between early complementary feeding and 12 months, establishing that an age-discriminating lipid feature is plausible; it does not report C30H30N4O3 or any specific compound matching it.

evidence.title: The potential role of early life feeding patterns in shaping the infant fecal metabolome: implications for neurodevelopmental outcomes
evidence.study_population: Human infants, fecal samples at 1 and 6 months, untargeted LC/HRMS metabolomics
evidence.relevance: Shows that many untargeted fecal metabolite features track milk-based feeding at younger ages (1-6 months), consistent with the general expectation that milk-associated features are higher at ~5 months than after diet diversification - but the feature C30H30N4O3 is not among any reported annotations.

evidence.title: Network-based representation learning reveals the impact of age (and diet) on fecal metagenomics and metabolomics during early complementary feeding (5-12 months) in U.S. formula-fed infants
evidence.study_population: U.S. formula-fed human infants, randomized controlled feeding trial, fecal metagenomics and metabolomics from 5 to 12 months
evidence.relevance: Closest available study design (same 5- vs 12-month contrast, fecal multi-omics) and confirms age is a dominant driver of fecal metabolite features in this window; however, it reports no compound with formula C30H30N4O3, so it provides only contextual, not feature-level, support.

evidence.title: BilR is a gut microbial enzyme that reduces bilirubin to urobilinogen
evidence.study_population: Human gut metagenomes including 4,296 infant metagenomes from the first year of life
evidence.relevance: Cited only as the basis for the speculative tetrapyrrole analogy: gut bilirubin-reducing capacity is low in early infancy and increases over the first year, which would predict higher unreduced tetrapyrrole-like species earlier. The formula C30H30N4O3 does not match bilirubin, biliverdin or urobilinoids, so this is background reasoning, not evidence for this feature.

caveats: The feature has no structural annotation - only an elemental formula from an untargeted lipidomics run - so literature-based evaluation is fundamentally limited: dozens of unrelated structures share C30H30N4O3, and any of them (including chromatographic artifacts, plasticizers/xenobiotics from formula packaging, or diet-derived compounds) could underlie the peak. Formula-only features cannot be validated against published metabolomics because most studies report named compounds, not raw formulas. MS/MS-based structural elucidation (or matching to an in-house/public spectral library, e.g. GNPS molecular networking) is required before any literature-based confidence assessment is meaningful. Also note that formula-level searching is intrinsically low-recall: a study could have reported the same molecule under a name without listing the formula in indexed text.
